summary: A BBN note observing that the FTP and Remote Job Entry protocols had grown very similar, each with a control connection for commands and a data connection for uninterpreted data. It suggests merging them into a single data transfer protocol and lists advantages beyond simplicity. It is a proposal, not a specification.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC proposes combining shared parts of FTP and Remote Job Entry in a common data-transfer protocol. Sites could implement file-transfer commands, job-execution commands, or both.

subtitle: A proposal to combine shared parts of FTP and Remote Job Entry.

tldr.problem: FTP and Remote Job Entry shared control, data transfer, identification, and parameter-setting functions.
tldr.mechanism: The author proposes a common data-transfer protocol with command groups for files and job execution.
tldr.outcome: The RFC suggests a possible path for revising FTP and RJE while aiming to minimize changes to existing implementations.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 486's status as Unknown. The RFC presents a proposal for a common data-transfer mechanism.

sections.title: Similarities Between FTP and RJE
sections.content:
Bob Bressler observes that FTP and Remote Job Entry (RJE) both use a control connection for commands and a data connection for uninterpreted data. Both also identify users, set parameters, and transfer data.

New ideas such as the hot card reader had been introduced in one protocol or the other, although the RFC says such concepts could apply to both.
sections.plainLanguage: FTP and RJE both use one connection for commands and another for data. The author says their shared features could be handled together.

sections.title: A Common Data-Transfer Protocol
sections.content:
The proposal suggests a single protocol with groups of general system commands, parameter settings, data controls, file operations, and job-execution commands. An implementation could support the file-transfer routines and commands without supporting job execution.

A site could reject unsupported commands with a command-not-implemented response. The author argues that sharing the common code could avoid separate FTP and RJE programs and connections.
sections.plainLanguage: A common protocol could have separate groups of commands for files and jobs. A site could support file transfer without implementing job execution.

sections.title: Storing Files and Running Jobs Separately
sections.content:
The RFC gives an example in which an RJE user stores a job's card deck on another machine using the file-transfer commands, then later connects to a batch server to run it. This would separate access to storage from access to a batch machine.

The author proposes using the forthcoming FTP specification as a starting point and revising RJE around a shared transfer component. He says the goal is not to put every function into one protocol, but to make common data-transfer mechanisms available.
sections.plainLanguage: A user could store job input on one machine and submit it to a batch server later. The proposal aims to share data-transfer functions, not combine every function.
